caption: Ever wondered why your ears pop on a plane?
Here's what's actually happening inside your head.
Behind your eardrum sits a tiny pocket of air - your middle ear.
On the ground, the pressure inside matches the air outside. Perfectly balanced.
But as the plane climbs, the cabin pressure drops.
The trapped air pushes outward, and your eardrum bulges, like a balloon.
Then a tiny tube to your throat - the Eustachian tube - cracks open.
Air escapes, the pressure evens out, and... POP!
The tube doesn't open on its own as easily, so your eardrum gets pushed inward.
That's why swallowing, yawning, or chewing gum helps - they pull the tube open.
